clue.text: Really Satanic, such discourse.

definitions.text: Really Satanic, such discourse

parts.words: Really Satanic, such discourse
parts.note: read literally, a conversation that is truly about Satan; really the idiom said when someone just mentioned turns up

explanation.surface: A remark that some piece of conversation is positively diabolical.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, said when the person being discussed appears, literally means chat concerning Satan.

clue.text: Knew again a way to fresh realisation

definitions.text: realisation

indicators.note: fresh suggests the letters of knew again are made over into something new

parts.words: Knew again

explanation.surface: Recognising someone again opens a route to new understanding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fresh' rearranges the nine letters of KNEW AGAIN; 'a way to' is linking padding.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden dawning of understanding is called an awakening, a synonym for coming to realise something.

clue.text: Where to find galley-slaves ashore?

definitions.text: Where to find galley-slaves ashore?

parts.words: Where to find galley-slaves ashore?
parts.note: a galley is a ship's cooking room, so those who toil over the cooking on land work in its domestic equivalent

explanation.surface: Asking where oarsmen chained to ancient ships would be found on dry land.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's galley is its cooking room; the household room for cooking is the land equivalent.

clue.text: That remote hearty state.

definitions.text: That remote hearty state.

parts.words: That remote hearty state.
parts.note: alludes to the proverb that absence makes the heart grow more affectionate, so being remote produces this condition of the heart

explanation.surface: A cryptic description of a cheerful frame of mind far away.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'absence makes the heart grow fonder' is the key: remote means absent.
explanation.definitionFit: By the proverb, a heart separated from a loved one grows more affectionate, the comparative of loving.

clue.text: Does, she keep on at little, Daniel, wretch?

definitions.text: Does, she keep on at little, Daniel, wretch?

parts.words: Does, she keep on at little, Daniel, wretch?
parts.note: a nagging woman might harry Dan, the short form of Daniel; said together those words run into the term for a scolding old woman

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a woman keeps nagging poor little Daniel.
explanation.walkthrough: To keep on at is to harry, and little Daniel is Dan; run together, HARRY DAN sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A harridan is a bad-tempered, scolding old woman, a wretch who nags.

clue.text: "All night — has the casement jess stirr'd To the dancers ——— in" (Tennyson).

definitions.text: "All night — has the casement jess stirr'd To the dancers ——— in" (Tennyson).

parts.words: "All night — has the casement jess stirr'd To the dancers ——— in" (Tennyson).
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Tennyson's poem Maud; the missing word follows the dancers

explanation.surface: A line from Tennyson with one word left blank for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: The line in Maud reads 'All night has the casement jessamine stirr'd To the dancers dancing in tune'; the print cuts jessamine and tune short.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation's gap is filled by the present participle describing what the revellers were doing.

clue.text: Quite a boy," no doubt thought Olivia.

definitions.text: Quite a boy," no doubt thought Olivia.

parts.words: Quite a boy," no doubt thought Olivia.
parts.note: in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night the countess Olivia falls for a heroine disguised as the youth Cesario

explanation.surface: Olivia admiring a young man.
explanation.walkthrough: In Twelfth Night, Olivia loves 'Cesario', really the heroine in disguise, so she would think her quite a boy.
explanation.definitionFit: The disguised heroine of Twelfth Night is the one Olivia takes for a young man.

clue.text: You may get a bull's-eye here.

definitions.text: You may get a bull's-eye here.

parts.words: You may get a bull's-eye here.
parts.note: a bull's-eye is a thick convex glass lens fitted to a lamp, not only the centre of a target

explanation.surface: Suggesting a place for a perfect shot at darts or archery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bull's-eye' suggests a target; a bull's-eye lantern has a thick rounded lens.
explanation.definitionFit: A bull's-eye lamp is a portable light with a domed glass lens.

clue.text: In which a player may run up and down the pitch.

definitions.text: In which a player may run up and down the pitch.

parts.words: In which a player may run up and down the pitch.
parts.note: a musician practises runs ascending and descending in musical pitch, not across a sports field

explanation.surface: A footballer running the length of the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'player' and 'pitch' suggest sport; they are a musician and musical pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Musical exercises of notes ascending and descending step by step are practised by instrumentalists.

annotationWithheld.clue: Doubtless how the pedestrian being sol

clue.text: The vermicular formation in battle

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'The vermicular formation in battle (5)': LEECH seems hidden in 'battle echelon', but the held text lacks the word supplying ECH.

clue.text: Knock out by mixing lime in teal

definitions.text: Knock out

indicators.note: mixing tells us to stir the letters of the phrase together into a new order

parts.words: lime in tea

explanation.surface: A drink spoiled by stirring citrus into it, knocking someone out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixing' rearranges LIMEINTEA; the nine-letter answer needs 'tea', so 'teal' is a misprint.
explanation.definitionFit: To eliminate a competitor is to knock them out of a contest, a sporting synonym.

clue.text: Like a half-starved dermatologist?

definitions.text: Like a half-starved dermatologist?

parts.words: Like a half-starved dermatologist?
parts.note: the adjective for very thin also reads as one who deals with skin, as a skin doctor does

explanation.surface: Wondering how a skin specialist who has gone hungry would look.
explanation.definitionFit: Very thin people are called skinny, and a dermatologist is a skin doctor, hence the pun.

clue.text: A nervy centre, and inside too.

definitions.text: A nervy centre, and inside too.

parts.words: A nervy centre, and inside too.
parts.note: a cluster of nerve cells forms a centre within the body, so it is both nervy and inside

explanation.surface: A jittery middle player who is also an inside forward.
explanation.definitionFit: A ganglion is a mass of nerve cells inside the body, a nerve centre.

clue.text: It's preceded, maybe, by the crash of a gate,

definitions.text: It's preceded, maybe, by the crash of a gate,

parts.words: It's preceded, maybe, by the crash of a gate,
parts.note: gate-crashing, arriving uninvited, comes before this unwelcome entry

explanation.surface: Something that follows a gate being smashed down.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'crash of a gate' is gatecrashing, turning up at a party uninvited.
explanation.definitionFit: Gatecrashing is an unwelcome entrance, an imposition on others' privacy.

clue.text: No, this doesn't mean drunk when flying!

definitions.text: No, this doesn't mean drunk when flying!

parts.words: No, this doesn't mean drunk when flying!
parts.note: tight is slang for drunk and air suggests flying, but the compound means sealed against leaks

explanation.surface: Denying that a word describes being intoxicated on a plane.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sealed so no gas can pass through is described with this compound.

clue.text: Singular movement of troops? in logic!

definitions.text: Singular movement of troops?
definitions.meaning: the science of moving and supplying troops is ..., so a singular form drops the s

definitions.text: in logic!
definitions.meaning: an old adjective meaning relating to logic or reasoning

explanation.surface: A peculiar troop manoeuvre that is somehow logical.
explanation.definitionFit: Military supply and movement is called logistics; the term also once meant concerning reasoning or calculation.

clue.text: Certainly not the sort to spin long yarn.

definitions.text: Certainly not the sort to spin long yarn.

parts.words: Certainly not the sort to spin long yarn.
parts.note: spinning a long yarn is telling a lengthy story; someone terse would never do it

explanation.surface: A person unlikely to sit at a spinning wheel making lengthy thread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spin long yarn' suggests textiles but means telling a long-winded tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Laconic speakers use very few words, so they never tell long stories.

clue.text: Position that affords a chance to get off!

definitions.text: Position
definitions.meaning: one's place or rank in life

definitions.text: that affords a chance to get off!
definitions.meaning: a stopping place where passengers may leave a train

explanation.surface: A post that offers an escape route.
explanation.definitionFit: Rank or standing is one's station in life; railway stops are also stations where travellers alight.

clue.text: She takes in the cat but not without

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'She takes in the cat but not without (6)' is cut short: S(CAT)HE is clear but the definition is missing.
annotationWithheld.clue: She takes in the cat but not without

clue.text: Anyhow I can't be put into such a closet.

definitions.text: such a closet

indicators.note: anyhow means in any haphazard order, so the letters of the phrase are rearranged

parts.words: I can't be

explanation.surface: Someone protesting they cannot be shut in a cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anyhow' rearranges the letters of I CAN'T BE; 'put into' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Closet once meant a small private room, and a cabinet is likewise a private chamber or cupboard.

clue.text: "O monstrous — buckram men own out of two." (K. Henry V, Pt. 1).

definitions.text: "O monstrous — buckram men own out of two." (K. Henry V, Pt. 1).

parts.words: "O monstrous — buckram men own out of two." (K. Henry V, Pt. 1).
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1 where Falstaff's attackers multiply in the telling

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare with a number left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Prince Hal's line is 'O monstrous! eleven buckram men grown out of two!'; the print loses the g of grown and an I from IV.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the number Falstaff's imaginary assailants in buckram swelled to.

clue.text: Green in Scotland, entailing perhaps a long drive.

definitions.text: Green in Scotland, entailing perhaps a long drive.

parts.words: Green in Scotland, entailing perhaps a long drive.
parts.note: the Scottish border village famed for runaway weddings, reached by eloping couples after a long journey

explanation.surface: A golf course in Scotland requiring a big tee shot.
explanation.walkthrough: Gretna Green, just over the Scottish border, was where eloping English couples drove to marry without parental consent.
explanation.definitionFit: The village's full name ends in Green, and lovers drove there from England to wed.

clue.text: Distinctive mark for reference perhaps.

definitions.text: Distinctive mark
definitions.meaning: a letter or symbol, or a distinguishing quality

definitions.text: reference perhaps
definitions.meaning: a written testimonial given to an employer about someone

explanation.surface: A distinguishing sign used to point a reader elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A written symbol or trait is one sense; an old term for a testimonial from an employer is another.

clue.text: There's room at the top here!

definitions.text: There's room at the top here!

parts.words: There's room at the top here!
parts.note: the saying about scope for advancement read literally as a room just under the roof

explanation.surface: The proverb that there is always room for ambitious people.
explanation.definitionFit: The topmost room of a house, under the roof, is a loft.

clue.text: Mr Punch advised wives to feed him!

definitions.text: Mr Punch advised wives to feed him!

parts.words: Mr Punch advised wives to feed him!
parts.note: the humorous magazine Punch popularised the advice to wives to feed their husband, called by a rude name

explanation.surface: The puppet Mr Punch giving domestic advice to wives.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch was a British humorous magazine; its catchphrase 'Feed the brute!' told wives how to keep husbands happy.
explanation.definitionFit: The catchphrase calls a hungry husband a savage beast.

clue.text: Traditional, occupation on a morning.

definitions.text: Traditional, occupation on a morning.

parts.words: Traditional, occupation on a morning.
parts.note: the folk rhyme about gathering nuts in May on a cold and frosty morning

explanation.surface: A customary job done first thing in the day.
explanation.walkthrough: The children's song 'Here we go gathering nuts in May' places the activity on a cold and frosty morning.
explanation.definitionFit: Gathering hazelnuts from hedges is the pastime named in the traditional song.

clue.text: In which he laughs last who lives longest.

definitions.text: In which he laughs last who lives longest.

parts.words: In which he laughs last who lives longest.
parts.note: twists the proverb about laughing last: in this scheme the final survivor takes the whole fund

explanation.surface: A version of the proverb that whoever laughs last laughs longest.
explanation.definitionFit: In this annuity scheme, members' shares pass to survivors until the last one alive collects everything.

clue.text: It isn't usually laid down as an to the shy.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'It isn't usually laid down as an to the shy. (7-7)' has a word missing after 'an'.
annotationWithheld.clue: It isn't usually laid down as an to the shy.
